Tawakoni

Tawakoni is a named historical people within the wider Wichita-affiliated account. A focused Handbook of Texas entry introduces particular Texas locations and diplomatic encounters, while the Wichita and Affiliated Tribes’ community history supplies a related institutional perspective. This guide keeps the name and its chronology distinct without asserting a separate present-day government.

01

Named locations and diplomatic encounters

Krieger’s account places Tawakoni communities on the lower Canadian River in 1719 and describes their later Texas range between present Waco and Palestine. It records visits by Athanase de Mézières in the 1770s and a Brazos River village identified in Juan Agustín Morfi’s 1781 account. These place descriptions are historical source summaries, not exact modern boundaries. The varying written spellings and relationships deserve comparison with the underlying encounter records.

Read the sources [1] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online

02

Reservation history in a wider community account

The entry discusses treaty-era relationships and the move across Red River in 1859 into the Wichita reservation setting. Its brief treaty summary is not substituted for the actual instruments or later legal history. The Tribe’s connected narrative names Tawakoni within the affiliated peoples while preserving a wider story of displacement and continuity. The Fort Belknap kitchen photograph gives nearby Brazos-reservation military context only; it does not identify a Tawakoni building, village, person or style of architecture.

Read the sources [1] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online [2] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey [3] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online

Tawakoni Indians ↗

Publication: Originally 1952; page metadata lists August 1, 1995 revision

Margery H. Krieger’s specifically Tawakoni account introduces named locations and diplomatic contacts, then reservation-era movement. It is a brief historical synthesis, not direct treaty inspection or a current-government account. Spellings and relationships should be compared across records rather than collapsed.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete three-paragraph main body, web lines 7–9, byline and publication/revision metadata read. Underlying Hodge reference, treaties and colonial visit reports were not inspected; no numerical or current legal claim adopted.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access note: Actual public HTML body readable without an account in this inspection. Linked bibliography, archival instruments and media remain separate works unless expressly listed.

Wichita Memories — four connected institutional history chapters ↗

Four linked chapters explain the Tribe’s historical account from early encounters through village life, displacement and continuing community. The credits identify a cooperative exhibit. Treat the chapters as one work, keep named historical groups distinct, and attribute archaeological, treaty and continuity interpretations rather than turning the narrative into independently checked archival evidence.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete main narratives of In the Beginning:1540–1750 (lines27–38), People of the Grass House:1750–1820 (27–39), Days of Darkness:1820–1934 (27–37), and A New Beginning:1934–Present (27–38), plus References and Contributors (27–91). Public narrative passages read; no quoted origin stories, ceremonial details, images or underlying bibliography reproduced or separately researched.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access note: Public readable English HTML, no account/paywall encountered. Individual publication/revision dates are unstated; date ranges in titles are historical coverage, not publication dates. Do not repeat historical population estimates as current figures, infer present identities from archaeological phases, or treat institutional treaty summaries as direct readings of the instruments.

Brazos Indian Reservation — selected location and Fort Belknap context ↗

Publication: Undated publication

Narrow supporting place context: this account places the Brazos Reservation twelve miles south of Fort Belknap and discusses troops from the fort at the reservation. The photographed fort kitchen is therefore nearby military/agency context, never a Kitsai or Tawakoni dwelling or the reservation itself. No jurisdiction or favorable colonial characterization is adopted.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Scope: Selected main-body location paragraphs, web lines 7–9, the Fort Belknap troop paragraph at 16 and the removal paragraph at 21 read. Only the fort/reservation location relationship supports image relevance. The longer article, its casualty totals and legal/jurisdiction claims are not adopted as independently verified history.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access note: Actual public HTML body readable without an account in this inspection. Linked bibliography, archival instruments and media remain separate works unless expressly listed.
